claims.text: A WVTaTiCr refractory high-entropy-alloy coating can be deposited by laser cladding onto a 42-CrMo steel substrate.
The laser-cladded WVTaTiCr coating is applicable to stainless-steel surfaces such as 304 stainless steel.
Increasing the Cr content up to the WVTaTiCr (Cr 1) formulation is the proposed coating modification.
Unmodified stainless steel or 42-CrMo steel has inherently limited corrosion resistance in extreme environments.
The coating can be evaluated by corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
The coating can be evaluated by high-temperature oxidation at 800 °C.
Laser cladding with high Cr content produces a refined dendritic microstructure.
The modified coating precipitates a corrosion-resistant Cr2Ta Laves phase.
The coating forms a uniform passive oxide film containing CrTaO4, TiO2, and Cr2O3.
Cr addition induces lattice distortion that promotes precipitation of the protective Laves phase.
Cr addition facilitates formation of a compact and uniform passive film.
The compact passive film reduces ionic diffusion and thereby limits corrosive attack.
The laser-cladded coating will significantly improve corrosion resistance relative to an unmodified substrate.
Coated samples will have lower corrosion current density and corrosion rate than untreated samples.
Coated samples will have improved high-temperature oxidation resistance and lower oxide weight gain than untreated samples.
The corrosion benefit depends on coating adhesion, Cr content, coating thickness, processing quality, and environmental severity.
Coating delamination or mechanical stress can reduce the corrosion-resistance benefit.
The magnitude of the improvement and the optimal Cr composition remain to be determined empirically.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in corrosion current density, corrosion rate, or oxide weight gain relative to an uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
